newsitem.title: USA: Rubin evinces scant concern about dollar's drop.
newsitem.headline: Rubin evinces scant concern about dollar's drop.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent

Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin evinced scant concern on Thursday about the recent abrupt drop of the dollar against the Japanese yen, leaving the door open, some analysts believe, to a further, eventual fall.
In remarks to the Investment Company Institute and later to reporters, Rubin reiterated his support for a strong dollar, saying it helped keep down inflation and interest rates.
But, in response to a reporter's question, he added that the dollar had been strong "for some time now."
At the very least, analysts said, that means that Rubin, who sets U.S. dollar policy, is not worried about the recent steep fall of the American currency against the yen.
"He's still comfortable with current levels," said Keith Woodfin of consultants Foreign Exchange Analytics.

Since the beginning of the month, the dollar has tumbled by more than 9 percent against the Japanese currency. In late New York trading, the dollar settled at 115.97 yen, down from 117.23 yen late Wednesday.

The dollar's steep fall has yet to have much impact on U.S. stock and bond markets, however. The latter is especially dependent on buying by Japanese investors. If the dollar fell too far, they would end up losing money and might pull some of their money out of the United States.

"Rubin and U.S. officials see little urgency in the foreign exchange market," said Marc Chandler of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell investment bank. "It (the dollar's fall) has not disrupted capital flows into the United States."

The dollar's decline in recent days has been triggered by shifting expectations in financial markets about the outlook for U.S. and Japanese interest rates. The higher the rate, the more lucrative a currency is for investors to hold.

Investors are no longer so confident that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates on May 20, nor are they as convinced as they were before that the Bank of Japan will keep its rates at rock bottom levels indefinitely.
The dollar's sharp drop also was triggered by jawboning by Japanese officials, who voiced concern that a weak yen would push up Japan's trade surplus. Rubin shared that concern.
But with the dollar's abrupt fall of recent days, Japanese officials have generally changed their tune and signalled their desire for currency stability.
Rubin, though, seemed to steer clear of seconding that sentiment. "I would still say we have had a strong dollar for some time now," he said at another point to reporters.

Those comments convinced some analysts that Rubin might not be perturbed by a further, gradual drop of the U.S. currency against the yen. "There's not going to be resistance to a further decline," Woodfin said.

Other analysts though argued that was reading too much into Rubin's remarks. The dollar, for its part, temporarily blipped higher on the Treasury chief's comments as traders focused on his continued backing for a strong U.S. currency.

A Clinton administration official, who declined to be identified, told Reuters earlier this week that he believed that the Treasury would be comfortable with a dollar/yen rate roughly in the 110/115 yen range. Other government agencies would probably prefer an even weaker U.S. currency, he said.
Rubin declined comment on the dollar's current level.
"We don't sashay around, we have a policy, we believe in it, we follow it," he said. "We don't adjust ourselves to day-to-day movements of the markets.
"I think a strong dollar increases confidence in our markets, which is good for the cost of capital, lowers inflation, lowers interest rates, and that is our policy."
